extracted.intended_audience: scholars, physicians, herbalists, and botanists (early/medieval-modern readers of natural history)
extracted.subtask_description: A classical botanical treatise excerpt that describes criteria for distinguishing, classifying, and judging plants (morphology, habitat, odors, saps, medicinal/toxic properties, propagation and useful parts). Intended to guide identification and assessment of plants and their remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant parts as classification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants are described and distinguished by their component parts: radix (root), truncus (trunk), rami (branches), folia (leaves), fructus (fruit), pediculus (pedicel), umbella, semina, flores, calyx, pericarpium, matrix/medulla, humor, lacryma, nodus, lanugo, nervus, fibra, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists these parts as the basis for many differences between trees and herbs; observers should note which parts are present and how they are formed (e.g., which part gives rise to shoots or seeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flower colour and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Flower colours (albi, rubet, croceos, aureum, nigros, virides, caeruleos, etc.) are important distinguishing features; plants may vary widely in floral colour even within related species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some species have white flowers, others red or yellow; some flowers may be black or very dark. Colour can indicate affinities (e.g., croceus vs viridis) and is linked to regional and seasonal causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of calyx (protective floral envelope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a flower has a calyx (calyx/adfiet) is meaningful: a calyx protects the thin floral substance before exposure to the sun; some flowers lack a calyx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The calyx is often like a leaf and is necessary before delicate floral tissues are developed and exposed to sunlight; its presence explains why most flowers have a calyx while some (e.g., 'Apollinis flori') do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality and flowering time (relation to climate and region)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a plant flowers (in cold or heat, in spring, at crepuscule/meridie) and whether it fruits early or late are diagnostic and linked to climate and regional conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some plants flower in cold weather and others in heat; flowering/fruiting order may vary (some fruits form before flowers or seed forms before petals); seasonality also affects medicinal selection by physicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evergreen vs deciduous habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a plant is fronde perpetua (evergreen) or loses leaves in winter is a distinguishing and functional property: evergreens are often 'calidiores' and preferred medicinally in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evergreen plants retain leaves through winter and are associated with warmer 'substantia' and are sometimes preferred by physicians; the habit is linked to the plant's native climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root quality and medicinal potency
rubrics_metrics.description: Roots and the uppermost root portions are often the most 'optima' medicinal parts; roots are nutritive and commonly used in remedies; the topmost part of the root (closest to germen) is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the rule that the part which lived (the living portion) contains the virtue; thus wooden (ligneous) parts may lack virtue except where they germinate. In roots, the superior/top part is typically most potent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sap/lac quality and indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Saps (lac, viscum, lacryma) differ in viscosity, fatness, translucence and odor; their qualities indicate usefulness (e.g., resinous, oily, tenax). Generation of viscous sap in roots often indicates particular properties and may coincide with vermes in roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good sap is translucent, coagulates slightly, is oily/fat, not overly burnt; the presence of worms where viscum forms is an indicator; mixing of root sap with larix lacrima or pitch alters properties. These tests are used to judge quality for medicinals and aromatic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aroma/odor as classificatory and qualitative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant's odor and taste (odorata, odore, sapor) are used to classify and judge its uses: strongly odorous plants (agallochum, cinnamon, nardus, crocus, etc.) are aromatic and often warm in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Odorous plants are further judged by whether their odor arises from a dry or humid principle; some odours indicate heating qualities and suitability for incense/perfume. The text explains that many 'aromata' are warm (calida) and that fragrance strength and behavior under fire (smoke vs powder) affect utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toxicity and poisonous qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain plants are poisonous (venena, venenofze), either by nature or through their sap/juice (e.g., black sap, putrid juices); some fruits/trees (e.g., 'mortis pomum') have deadly juices but may become harmless in different regions or after processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toxicity may depend on region, processing, or ripeness; some plants that are poisonous in origin are innocuous when transplanted. Observers should note habitat and preparation history when judging toxicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and soil influence on plant character
rubrics_metrics.description: The place where a plant grows (marshes, sands, rocks, mountains, near mines or metallic veins, in aprici or umbra) strongly affects its qualities: color, scent, succulence, and medicinal potency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: plants near metal workings or in marshes often become discoloured or foul-smelling; those on warm sunny soils tend to be larger and more succulent; physicians prefer mountain-grown plants. The text emphasizes regional variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation and origin (spontaneous, transplanted, by grafting, from cuttings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a plant is spontaneous (sponté proueniunt), transplanted (feruntur), or propagated by grafting/inoculation affects its behaviour and qualities; some varieties arise by grafting (infitione), cuttings, or natural runners (repunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plants propagated by grafting may change form (e.g., citrus into apple producing 'Adami malus') and virtues can be transferred or altered by propagation technique; propagation method is therefore diagnostic for identity and expected virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of development: seed, flower, fruit (reproductive timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing of seed, flower and fruit development varies: sometimes seed/female parts are generated before the flower; fruits can precede flowers in maturation (femus ex tertea parte concocta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering affects fertility and preservation of the generative power; the text discusses why female organs may be more matured early to preserve their 'vir' (genital power) during confection and exposure to humidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wood buoyancy and physical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Wood floats or sinks in water depending on its density and the contained air; rarer (more airy) wood tends to float, compact wood sinks; pieces fall and orient according to density and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations are given about why some wood sinks upright in deep water and why anchors/ropes are used to keep vessels steady. Observers should consider internal air and robustness when judging timber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of plant quality by sensory tests (clarity, fatness, non-burnt)
rubrics_metrics.description: For saps/resins/aromatics the best are those that are translucent, coagulate (confittit), are fatty/oily, not over-burnt (minimé adustis), and emit the proper smoke (fumus) rather than being mere powder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes sensory criteria (sight of translucence, tactile fatness, smell when heated) for ranking materials for incense and medicine; different materials behave differently under fire (some should not be burned to powder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of drying, heating and processing on virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Drying, roasting, heating, or other processing changes a plant's virtues and odors: some substances lose or gain potency when dried or smoke-extracted (e.g., lac can be cooked down until it coagulates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that drying may make some aromatics better and that aqueous humidity can prevent odors; processing methods are essential to produce desirable products (e.g., extracting lac, preparing incense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between plant 'substance' thickness and odor
rubrics_metrics.description: Thicker-substantiated plants (crassa substantia) are more odoriferous when dried and produce better incense; very thin substances often lack lasting odor and are less suited for aromatic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus some trees, rather than herbs, are preferred for odorous materials because their longer-lasting, thicker bodies yield more persistent fragrance and resins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate influence on plant stature and succulence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants in warm and humid regions tend to be larger and more succulent; in cold or dry regions they are smaller and drier though sometimes more potent (frigidae may be stronger in certain virtues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises expecting regional variation: a plant's size and succulence reflect climate and affect its medicinal efficacy; some cold-region plants (e.g., cicuta in humid shade) can be unexpectedly powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaf density, shade and harmful vapours
rubrics_metrics.description: Dense-leaved trees that give much shade (e.g., walnut, nucis) may generate noxious vapours beneath them that can affect sleepers and cause maladies; shade proximity can cause harmful effects unrelated to the shadow itself but to proximity to the tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: in regions where people sleep under such trees, sickness may result; caution is advised regarding habitation and storage under dense-canopied trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and species distinctions for incense/resin value
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all species of a genus yield equal lac/odor; e.g., different species of thuris/abietes produce different lacrimae; certain geographic provenances (e.g., Ethiopian, Libanian) are prized and may be used by kings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The source, species, and local cultivation all affect resin quality and market value; collectors should note provenance as an important criterion of quality.
